list.listitem: Regular screening by an opthalmologist, especially for adults over age 55 years, is recommended according to AAO guidelines. C
A combination of high-dose vitamin C, vitamin E, beta-carotene, and zinc slows disease progression except in smokers. A
High-dose antioxidants and lutein slow progression of disease. A
Wet age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) can be treated with anti-VEGF injections. A
Dry ARMD cannot be treated. C

background.definition: ARMD is a degenerative disorder of the retina (macula) affecting patients age 55 years and older that produces central visual impairment. It is composed of two disease types: dry and wet.

list.listitem: 14.3% 15-year cumulative incidence of early ARMD.
1.3% 15-year cumulative incidence of late ARMD (includes end-stage dry disease and wet disease).
A systematic review concluded that the annual incidence of late AMD in American whites age 50 years and older was 3.5/1000 persons.
Incidence increases with age (0.3/1000/year in persons 50 to 59 years, up to 37/1000/year in persons 90 years or older.
ARMD varies by racial and ethnic group: white 5.4%, Asian 4.6%, Hispanic 4.2%, and black 2.4%.
The differences in prevalence were not affected by age, gender, smoking, alcohol, diabetes, and hypertension status.
In patients with wet ARMD, nearly half required low-vision rehabilitation, and approximately 10% received social benefits (disability and pension, housing and taxes, transportation subsidies).
ARMD is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss.
In the United States, 8 million persons have monocular/binocular intermediate or monocular advanced ARMD.
The exact etiology of ARMD is unknown; the disease process is probably multifactorial.
Long-term aspirin use slightly increases the risk of age-related macular degeneration (NNH = 125).
Risk factors are shown in the table.
Aging retinal pigmented epithelium and diminished retinal perfusion leads to cell death and accumulation of waste products seen clinically as drusen.
Continued cell death results in vision loss and geographic atrophy.

Wet disease develops when cracks in Bruch's membrane allows for neovascular complexes to grow beneath the choroid or the retina. The resultant exudation of lipids and hemorrhage lead to further cell death and vision loss. Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) will eventually form fibrovascular scars that produce profound, irreversible vision loss and tissue destruction.

Comprehensive eye exam with biomicrosopic screening is recommended by guidelines from the American Academy of Ophthalmology every 5 to 10 years for patients without risk factors aged up to 40 years, every 2 to 4 years aged between 40 and 54, every 1 to 3 years aged between 55 and 64, and every 1 to 2 years aged over age 64. C

The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine screening for impaired visual acuity in older adults. This I statement was reaffirmed in 2022, with the supporting systematic review finding no clinical benefit in studies comparing screening with no screening.C
Vitamin E and gingko biloba, statins, carotenoids and omega-e fatty acids, and antioxidant combinations do not prevent ARMD in asymptomatic patients.A

To slow progression of disease, patients with macular degeneration should eat a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, stop smoking, and take a beta-carotene, vitamin E, and vitamin C combination supplement. This has been shown to slow progression for moderate to severe disease. B
A meta-analysis found an association between physical activity and a reduced risk of both early and late macular degeneration, but it is not clear if this is causal.
A Cochrane review concluded that there was insufficient evidence to determine whether there was a benefit bo blue light filtering intra-ocular lenses.
Patients with dry disease may complain about slowly progressive vision loss or metamorphopsia (wavy lines). Patients with wet disease may notice an acute loss of vision. C
Obtain fluorescein angiogram for diagnosis of wet ARMD.C

Central acuity loss is similar; ophthalmoscopic appearance is diagnostic
Central acuity affected, looks similar to ARMD but occurs at earlier age

list.listitem:
International classification and grading system for ARM and AMD:
Patients must be at least 55 years of age. Dry ARMD: retinal pigmented epithelium changes and atrophy, retinal pigment abnormalities, and soft drusen. Wet ARMD: retinal pigment epithelial detachments, subretinal neovascular membranes, subretinal hemorrhage, and/or hard exudates. The findings associated with dry ARMD may also be seen in wet disease.
Patients with dry disease may complain about slowly progressive vision loss or metamorphopsia (wavy lines). Patients with wet disease may notice an acute loss of vision.
Visual acuity in all patients may be diminished, and patients may have distortion when using an Amsler grid.
Dilated ophthalmoscopy may reveal retinal hemorrhage, drusen, and pigmentary changes in the macula.
Patients with newly diagnosed ARMD should have a careful history for smoking, medication, and supplement use; family history of ARMD and other visual problems; and any other ocular symptoms.
Color fundus photography allows for careful inspection of the macula and will rule in or rule out ARMD with fair accuracy.

Patients suspected of having disease may undergo optical coherence tomography or fluorescein angiographic imaging to detect the presence of choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Fluorescein angiography will highlight areas of retinal and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy not necessarily evident clinically. Fluorescein angiography also reveals subretinal neovascularization, which is diagnostic of wet ARMD and aids in determining treatment strategy.

Optical coherence tomography provides a two-dimensional in vivo cross section of the macula to evaluate severity of wet ARMD, to determine the frequency of follow-up visits, and to follow response to treatment.

A diagnostic accuracy study compared multiple tests for early detection of neovascular macular degeneration in the unaffected second eye using fundus fluorescein angiography as the reference standard. Fundus clinical examination (LR+ 22, LR- 0.5) and optical coherence tomography (LR+ 7.5, LR- 0.09) were most accurate, while simple visual acuity and self-reported vision were not helpful.

A systematic review of 10 studies with 1890 eyes found that Amsler grid testing was 67% sensitive and 99% specific (LR+ 67, LR- 0.33) for diagnosing neovascular ARMD when controls were health participants without visual complaints, but only 71% sensitive and 63% specific (LR+ 1.9, LR- 0.46) when controls were patients with non-neovascular ARMD.
A teleretinal program can identify patients with retinal problems, including macular degeneration.

A mobile application that can be used at home to monitor visual acuity in patients with macular degeneration had good sensitivity and specificity (93% and 92%, respectively) compared with Amsler grid findings.
If visually symptomatic and/or patient has signs of drusen, subretinal fluid or hemorrhage, lipid exudates, or RPE elevation, obtain a fluorescein angiogram.

If no signs of subretinal hemorrhage, subretinal fluid, exudate, or RPE elevation and if no dye leakage is present on fluorescein angiogram, dry ARMD may be diagnosed. If dye leakage is present, then wet disease is diagnosed, and the location of the CNV lesion needs to be determined (subfoveal, juxtafoveal, extrafoveal).
For subfoveal lesions and possibly some juxtafoveal lesions, treatment with anti-VEGF agents or PDT is warranted.
For some juxtafoveal and extrafoveal lesions, treatment with thermal laser photocoagulation is advisable.
Anti-VEGF injections are first-line agents to treat wet ARMD. A
A combination of high-dose vitamin C, vitamin E, beta-carotene, and zinc slows disease progression except in smokers. A
Lutein is effective in men with ARMD. B

Ranibizumab is recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody Fab that targets VEGF-A. Patients receving ranibizumab were more likely to lose fewer than 15-letters of vision (95% vs. 62%, NNT = 3) and more likely to gain vision (25% vs. 5%, NNT = 5). It is administered every 4 weeks intravitreally, and complication rates are similar to those for pegaptanib. Improvement can continue for as long as 12 months following the initiation of treatment.
A port delivery system has been developed for ranibizumab. While preferred over monthly injections in a trial, both treatment arms had high levels of satisfaction.
A network meta-analysis of 26 studies with 10,821 patients compared ranibizumab treatment regimens and concluded that ranibizumab 0.5 mg treat and extend was most effective.

A systematic review found 21 trials with 9557 patients that evaluated harms of intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor monoclonal antibodies, and found no evidence of increased risk of major cardiovascular events or non-ocular hemorrhage.
An RCT randomized 281 patients with wet ARMD to ranibizumab 0.5 mg or aflibercept 2.0 mg via intravitreal injection. At one year, there was no significant difference between groups.

Faricimab inhibts both vascular endothelial growth factor and angiopoietin-2. Two trials randomized 1329 patients to intravitreal faricimab 6 mg up to every 16 weeks or aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks. Faricimab was non-inferior to aflibercept.

A study randomized patients to aflibercept 8 mg every 12 weeks, 8 mg every 16 weeks, or 2 mg every 8 weeks (standard dose). The higher dose, less frequent regiimens were non-inferior to the standard regimen.

A Cochrane review concluded baed on 13 studies (largely influenced by the single American AREDS trial) that a combination of high-dose vitamin C, vitamin E, beta-carotene, and zinc may reduce the likelihood of disease advancement in patients with early ARMD (OR 0.72; 95% CI, 0.58-0.90). This corresponds to 4 fewer cases of progression to late ARMD for every 1000 people with early AMD at low risk of progression taking it (range 1 to 6), but increases to 78 fewer cases per 1000 for those with intermediate ARMD who are at higher risk of progression (range 26 to 126). It should be avoided in patients who smoke tobacco, as beta-carotene + vitamin E have been shown to increase mortality in smokers.
Because of this increase in the risk of lung cancer with beta-carotene, it has been successfully replaced with lutein/zeaxanthin in current formulations.
A 5-year study of 90 men found that lutein 10 mg daily improves vision in men with ARMD. This is often an ingredient in antioxidant combinations directed at patients with macular degeneration.

Pegaptanib sodium is a 28-base ribonucleic acid aptamer that binds and blocks activity of extracellular VEGF-165. It has been shown to reduce the risk of 15-letter vision loss and reduce the risk of severe vision loss. Patients receiving pegaptanib sodium were more likely to maintain or gain vision than those patients in the control group (33% vs. 23%, NNT = 10) and more likely to lose less than 15 letters of vision (70% vs. 15%, NNT = 6). It is administered intravitreally every 6 weeks. Serious complications in a 48-week study included endophthalmitis (1.3%), retinal detachment (0.6%), and traumatic lens injury (0.7%).

In a randomized trial, intravitreal aflibercept did not reduce the likelihood that patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration would convert to exudative age related macular degeneration.
There is no evidence that statins or steroids are effective at delaying the onset or progression of ARMD.
A retrospective cohort study found no assocation between use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs and visual acuity in patients with age-related macular degeneration.

A small RCT (n = 48) found a slowing in the growth of the size of the area affected by macular atrophy with topical isopropyl unoprostone in patients with age-related dry macular atrophy and age-related macular degeneration.
A small RCT (n = 33) randomized men with dry ARMD to IV aloprostadil 60 mcg or placebo for 3 weekis. They found a small improvement in visual lines, but further study is needed.
A substudy of the ASPREE randomized trial found no impact of low dose aspirin on progression of ARMD.

A study randomized 56 patients with submacular hemorrhage due to neovascular ARMD to sham injection, perfluoropropane injection (C3F8), tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) injection, or injectioin of both TPA and C3F8. Those in the TPA groups had better best corrected visual acuity at 3 months.

Thermal laser photocoagulation of choroidal neovascularization (CNV) was the first treatment available for wet ARMD. Although visual outcomes are better than the natural course of the disease, treatment of subfoveal disease leads to immediate vision loss and scotoma. This treatment is now reserved for juxtafoveal and extrafoveal disease only. A Cochrane review of 11 studies with 2159 participants, of generally low risk of bias, concluded that photocoagulation reduced drusen (OR 9.2; 95% CI, 6.3-13.4). The impact on the likelihood of CNV was modest, estimated to be a 1.4% absolute reduction in risk from a baseline of 8.3%.

Photodynamic therapy with verteporfin (PDT) is effective for the treatment of predominantly classic subfoveal CNV. This treatment is still used but has fallen out of favor with the advent of anti-VEGF agents.
Submacular surgery for CNV does not improve visual outcomes at 24 months and is not recommended.
A single study with 50 patients compared full macular translocation with photodynamic therapy. While it may be effective, serious complications are relatively common.
A Cochrane trial identified only one small study (n = 60) of cataract surgery in patients with ARMD, which suggested that surgery was safe and effective in these patients.
Another study with 82 eyes also concluded that cataract surgery was safe, with no worsening of wet ARMD in the surgical group.

A Cochrane review found two small trials of gingko biloba found positive effects, but evidence insufficient to recommend these drugs for patients with ARMD. Adequately powered, well-designed studies are needed.
Consultation with an occupational therapist specialized in low-vision rehabilitation may be required for patients with significant vision loss.
Self-rated depression in patients with ARMD correlates to severity of vision loss.
Consider referral for counseling and be vigilant for signs of depression in patients with visual loss.
A small trial randomized patients with exudate ARMD to gene therapy (n = 24) or control (n = 13). There was no difference between groups after 3 years.
A Cochrane review concluded that evidence was inconclusive (2 small RCTs) regarding the efficacy of photobiomodulation for non-exudative ARMD.

A trial randomized 274 patients to stereotactic radiotherapy or sham radiotherapy. The group receiving radiotherapy required fewer subsequent injections of an anti-VGEF drug (10.7 vs 13.3 over 2 years).
Treatment with anti-VEGF agents and PDT with verteporfin can be for as long as 2 years; beyond that clinical trials are lacking.
Patients who are at least 55 years of age or have visual complaint such as vision loss or distortion should be referred to an ophthalmologist.
Left untreated, wet ARMD will result in irreversible central vision loss due to fibrovascular scar formation. A
Prompt referral to an ophthalmologist will lead to earlier detection and treatment of disease, potentially saving central vision. C
Dry ARMD produces central vision loss and may become profound if geographic atrophy develops.

Dry ARMD may convert to wet ARMD if CNV develops. Left untreated, CNV produces subretinal hemorrhage and lipid exudation that is toxic. Additionally the CNV complex will develop into a fibrovascular scar, producing irreversible tissue damage and vision loss.
No treatment is restorative, but some patients who receive anti-VEGF therapy do obtain small improvements in acuity.
The majority of patients reach visual stabilization, and some patients still lose vision despite therapy.
In dry ARMD, use of the Amsler grid and regular ophthalmologic examination are necessary. The frequency of examination is determined by disease severity, patient needs, and physician discretion.

In wet ARMD, more regular evaluation is required to monitor for recurrence of CNV. Fluorescein angiography, indocyanine green angiography, and optical coherence tomography can be employed to check for and evaluate CNV presence and degree of activity.
Eat a diet rich in fruits and vegetables.
Stop smoking.
Have regular evaluation using the Amsler grid.
Take vitamin supplement listed in drug therapy section to slow progression of intermediate and advanced disease.
